To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the task technology fit approach helped to improve the usability and fit of an electronic patient portal, but that patients often do not start with a well-developed understanding of their personal health information management tasks.

1) the usability of the patient portal improved over the course the iterative development, 2) the portal fit with patient work improved over the course, but there was still room for improvement, 3) patients did not always know what tasks they could perform on the portal, 4) patients often had difficulty setting up proxy accounts, and 5) patients did not know how to use a proxy account.

the iterative development and evaluation of an electronic patient portal for a hospital discharge summary improved the portal’s fit to patient needs, and that patients’ lack of understanding of tasks that could be accomplished with the portal was a barrier to usability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how patient work is accomplished in the context of the patient portal.
the development of an approach to designing patient-centered electronic health records (EHRs) and electronic patient portals that are usable, useful, and fit the tasks and needs of patients.
the usability of electronic patient portals and how they fit with patients' work.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the task technology framework is an effective tool for evaluating and developing patient portals.
patient portal development should be informed by a task technology fit model.
patient portal developers can benefit from applying the task technology fit framework for evaluation and development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the portal is a good tool for patients who already know how to use it, but it is not a good tool for teaching patients how to use it.
usability testing of patient portals should be conducted from a patient perspective, and the testing should be conducted in an iterative fashion.

usability and task technology fit can be improved through iterative development, but that patient work and patient education are critical factors in designing a patient portal that is fit to the tasks that patients actually need to do.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the task technology fit approach can help improve the usability of health information technology for patient use.
the task technology fit framework can be used to help evaluate the fit of an electronic patient portal to patient work.
patient portal usability is an important issue that needs to be addressed by developers and evaluators.
